intro:
Regulars call because they trust your food and your people. The best way to handle repeat phone orders from regular customers is to make the reorder short, familiar, and accurate.

That means you ask only for what changed, confirm the name and number, and send the kitchen a clean ticket. If you use [ROAL](/how-it-works), it can answer the phone, take the order from your live menu, and keep the call moving without making your staff start from zero every time.

sections.h2: What should you ask when a regular customer calls back?
sections.body:
For repeat phone orders regular customers place, do not rebuild the whole order unless you need to. Start with the name, then ask what is different today. That saves time and helps the caller feel known.

A simple reorder flow works well for pizza shops, delis, and takeout spots:

1. "Hi, thanks for calling. Is this the same order as last time?"
2. "What would you like to change today?"
3. "What name should I put the order under?"
4. "What number can we reach you at if we need anything?"
5. "Your pickup will be ready in about 20 minutes. Does that work?"

If the customer says, "Same as usual," still confirm the important parts. For example: "You want the large pepperoni, extra cheese, no onions, and two sides of ranch, correct?" That takes 10 seconds and avoids a remake later.

You can also keep a short repeat-order checklist by the phone:
- Name
- Callback number
- Usual items
- Changes today
- Allergies or notes
- Pickup or delivery
- Ready time

ROAL can handle this kind of reorder from the live menu, and it will not offer items marked sold out.

sections.h2: How do you turn a familiar call into a fast reorder?
sections.body:
Regular callers often want speed more than conversation. The trick is to make the first 15 seconds do the work. If your staff or phone host sounds confident and organized, the caller usually follows along.

Use a script that makes the caller feel recognized:

"Welcome back. Are you ordering your usual, or is anything changing today?"

Then narrow it down. If the caller only wants one item changed, do not restart the whole order. Say:

"I have your usual family meal here. Do you want the same sides, or should I swap one out?"

Here is a simple example you can copy and swap for your own menu. Say a regular order is a $28 average order:

| Part of the call | Time-saving approach |
| --- | --- |
| Greeting | Ask if it is the usual order |
| Items | Confirm only changed items |
| Notes | Repeat allergies, sauces, and sides |
| Ready time | Give one clear pickup estimate |
| Close | Repeat the total and name |

If you get ten repeat calls a day and each one saves even a minute, that is ten minutes back in the rush. More important, your counter team stays focused on the line instead of the phone. ROAL is useful here because it can answer the order, confirm it back, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen without making the caller wait for a long back-and-forth.

sections.h2: How do you keep the kitchen from getting confused?
sections.body:
Regular customers are great until a small change gets missed. The kitchen needs one clean ticket, not a memory test. That is especially true when a caller says, "It’s my usual," but then adds extra sauce, a missing topping, or a side swap.

A good phone order ticket should capture the exact changes in the same order every time:

- Caller name
- Callback number
- Item name and size
- Modifiers
- Notes
- Pickup or delivery
- Ready time

Use one kitchen rule: if it matters to the cook, it belongs on the ticket. If it matters to the cashier, it belongs on the ticket too. If it is only a friendly note, keep it out of the line item.

Example:
- "Large chicken parm hero, no cheese on one half, extra sauce on the side, ready at 6:15"

That is easier to read than a long paragraph.

sections.h2: What if the regular asks for something you cannot do?
sections.body:
Repeat customers sometimes ask for special treatment because they know your shop. Be polite, but keep the same rules for everyone. That avoids confusion and makes the reorder easier to manage.

A few common examples:

- Sold-out item: "I’m sorry, that item is sold out today. I can offer the closest available option."
- Allergy question: "I want to make sure we handle that correctly, so I’m going to pass this to the staff with a note."
- Manager request: "I’ll send this to the team with your name and number."
- Catering-sized order: "I’m going to hand this to staff so we can make sure we have enough time and product."

Here is a practical handoff checklist:
1. Capture the name and callback number.
2. Repeat the request in plain English.
3. Add the reason for the handoff.
4. Tell the caller someone will follow up.

That is enough for your staff to step in without asking the customer to start over. It also keeps your phone flow calm during rush periods. ROAL is built to hand off catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests with a summary, so the staff gets the context fast.

sections.h2: How should you handle reorders during a rush?
sections.body:
Rush hour is where repeat phone orders regular customers place can either help or hurt. If the call is quick and clean, it keeps the line moving. If it turns into a long memory exercise, it slows the room down.

Use this rush-time playbook:

1. Answer with a short greeting.
2. Ask whether it is a repeat order.
3. Confirm only the changes.
4. Give one ready time.
5. End with a full repeat of the order name and pickup time.

Example script:
"Thanks for calling. Is this your usual order, or are we changing something today?"

If you use [Pickup order taking](/use-cases/pickup-orders) as your main phone flow, keep the phone order process separate from table work and front-counter questions. That way, the person on the line does not get buried under walk-in traffic.

A rough cost example can help you judge the value. Say your repeat phone order brings in a $28 ticket. If three repeat calls a day are lost because nobody can answer, that is $84 in sales potential for the day, using your own average order amount. Plug in your own number and compare it with the cost of your phone setup, staffing, and delivery app commissions.

sections.h2: What should regular customers hear when they call back next time?
sections.body:
The goal is not to sound robotic. The goal is to sound prepared. Regulars should hear that your shop remembers the pattern of the order, even if the exact items change.

A good repeat-order experience sounds like this:

"Hi, thanks for calling. Are you placing the same order as last time?"

If yes:

"Great. I have your usual here. What would you like to change today?"

If no:

"No problem. I’ll take it from the top."

That approach works because it gives the customer a shortcut without trapping them in it. Some people want the same wings, same sides, same sauce. Others want a new combo but still appreciate fast service.

To make that possible, keep your menu, hours, and address current. ROAL reads public menu pages, menu PDFs, menu photos, and website details when you set it up. Owners can also upload a menu in any format. Then you can test-call the host in the browser before you go live.

A simple quality checklist for repeat callers:
- Name sounds right
- Number is captured
- Last order is confirmed or updated
- Special instructions are repeated back
- Ready time is clear
- Kitchen ticket matches the call

sections.h2: How do you set up your phone line for easy reorders?
sections.body:
You do not need a big setup to make repeat orders easier. You need a phone setup that gets the call to the right place, plus a clear reorder flow.

If you want to forward calls, confirm the exact code with your carrier or phone system first and test with a call. On many landlines and some carriers, dial *72 then the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off. On some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set this in the web portal.

A practical setup list:
- Decide whether all calls forward or only busy/unanswered calls
- Test the forward with your own phone
- Make sure the kitchen screen shows the ticket clearly
- Keep the restaurant’s main number the same
- Turn forwarding off when you need to

With ROAL, each location gets its own phone line automatically after you claim the host, and you forward your existing number to it. That lets regular customers keep calling the number they already know, while the reorder process becomes simpler behind the scenes.

If you want to try it, [build a free test host](/try) from your website or Google Maps link and call it right in the browser.

takeaways: Ask regular callers what changed, not the whole order from scratch.
Use one clean script for name, callback number, items, and ready time.
Send every important change to the kitchen in a simple ticket format.
Keep repeat orders fast during rush hour with a short reorder flow.
Forward your existing number carefully and test it with a real call.

faq.q: How do I take repeat phone orders from regular customers faster?
faq.a: Start by asking whether it is the usual order, then confirm only the changes. Keep the caller’s name, phone number, and ready time in the same flow every time. That short script is easier for staff and less frustrating for regulars.

faq.q: What should I save for a regular phone order?
faq.a: Save the caller’s name, callback number, usual items, sizes, modifiers, and any notes that matter to the kitchen. If the customer has allergy concerns or special instructions, repeat them back before ending the call. That helps prevent mistakes on the ticket.

faq.q: How do I forward my restaurant phone for reorder calls?
faq.a: Call forwarding codes vary by carrier and plan, so confirm the exact code with your provider and test it. Some systems use *72 and *73 for landlines, while some mobile carriers use codes like **21*number# or **61*number#. Business VoIP systems often use a web portal.
